transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-20 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Rahul (Redwood SE), Maya (Goldenrod Head of ML), Ethan (CTO), Jordan (Infra)

Summary: intake/discovery focused on unit economics and deploy options (hosted vs dedicated vs private) and what levers move cost (batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization). Customer has a hard budget cap for Q3 POC and needs clarity on tradeoffs and an actual benchmark run.

Topics: pricing bands, batching tradeoffs, caching impact, dedicated commit sizing, SSO/KMS/audit requirements, pilot timeline

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Martinez: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro - i'm sofia, account lead. rahul is our se, he'll cover perf and benchmarks. can we go around real quick?
[00:08] Maya Lin: maya, head of ml at goldenrod. we're evaluating inference options for a client-facing assistant, lots of short prompts, high qps bursts.
[00:14] Ethan Park: ethan, cto. budget constraint is the primary gating factor.
[00:18] Jordan Reeves: jordan, infra. we'll own networking and security for any private deploy.
[00:22] Sofia Martinez: great. rahul, i'll hand over to you for a quick rundown on how levers change unit cost.
[00:27] Rahul Desai: cool. so at a high level, we look at three deployment modes: hosted api, dedicated reserved pools, and private/vpc or on-prem. hosted is fastest to spin up — pay as you go, per-token and per-embedding pricing. dedicated is capacity you reserve monthly, so per-token effectively drops for steady workloads. private moves the infra cost to you but can be better at scale if you have ops bandwidth.
[00:46] Rahul Desai: for numbers, to give a rough bracket — hosted per-token for a mid-size gen model sits somewhere in the order of magnitude of three to seven e-4 USD per input+output token depending on model and prompt length and whether streaming or not, but that varies. dedicated commits can reduce effective unit cost by 25 to 60% depending on utilization and model mapping.
[01:12] Maya Lin: when you say three to seven e-4, is that for something like a 7b open model? what about larger ones?
[01:17] Rahul Desai: it's a rough bracket. smaller quantized models are on the lower end, larger dense or newer models hit the higher end. plus sequence length matters — 2K context vs 8K changes kernel selection and memory ops.
[01:28] Ethan Park: can you explain the effect of batching and caching — realistically how much do we save?
[01:33] Rahul Desai: sure. two levers: batching aggregates requests to improve throughput (so lower tokens cost per second) but can add queuing/latency. caching — prefix or KV caching — avoids recomputing earlier tokens for repeated prompts. in many customer workloads with repeated prefixes or system messages, caching reduces token generation by 30-70% on the effective billable tokens. batching can give ~20-50% throughput improvements depending on model and batch size before you see latency spikes.
[02:00] Jordan Reeves: you mentioned kv cache — is that something in hosted or only in dedicated/private?
[02:05] Rahul Desai: we support KV/prefix caching across modes; hosted has managed caching and smart eviction, dedicated gives you more control over TTLs and cache warmup strategies, private gives full control but you manage ops. also note that caching effectiveness depends heavily on prompt patterns.
[02:18] Maya Lin: our prompts are mostly short, many templated system messages, and then user-specific few-shot context. sounds like caching could be big.
[02:24] Sofia Martinez: quick practical example: if you have a templated system prompt that stays constant for 80% of requests, caching that prefix could cut billable tokens dramatically.
[02:32] Ethan Park: okay, what about burst capacity? we have daily peaks at market open, 2-3x baseline for 15-20 minutes.
[02:37] Rahul Desai: hosted supports burst up to a point, but dedicated has predictable throughput and you can configure burst pools. for sporadic high peaks, a hybrid routing approach is typical: route normal traffic to dedicated for base load and failover or overflow to hosted during peaks — that keeps latency and cost predictable.
[02:55] Maya Lin: do you have a sample cost calc? like if i run 1M requests/day average, average 60 tokens generated per request, what does that look like?
[03:03] Rahul Desai: rough calc: 1M requests * 60 tokens = 60M tokens. at $0.0005/token that'd be $30k (this is simplified). with effective caching that removes 40% of generated tokens, you're down to ~36M tokens -> $18k; dedicated commit might reduce further depending on utilization and the commit price, say another 30% reduction on unit cost, so maybe in the low-teens thousands. again these are examples.
[03:30] Ethan Park: when you say commit price, is that a flat monthly for x throughput? do you guys do annual?
[03:36] Sofia Martinez: yes we have monthly/annual reserved pools. we do committed monthly/annual contracts with tiers for GPU types. annual gives better pricing. also committed burst windows and autoscale options.
[03:45] Jordan Reeves: security — we need SOC2, audit logs, SSO (SAML/OIDC), and customer-managed KMS. is that all supported?
[03:52] Rahul Desai: yes — hosted supports SOC 2, SAML/OIDC, audit logs. for KMS we provide integration options; dedicated and private give you stronger controls for keys and VPC peering. i'll drop the security pack in the follow-up.
[04:02] Maya Lin: any compliance caveats for storing cache or logs? we need to ensure no pii left for longer than 30 days.
[04:08] Rahul Desai: we can configure retention policies and scrub logs; dedicated/private makes retention enforcement easier. we'll include specifics in the security doc.
[04:15] Sofia Martinez: quick note — some customers worry about small-word mis-transcription: our examples show some product names get mangled by the transcribers in these notes, so we'll also provide the deck as a pdf.
[04:25] Ethan Park: competitor question: how are you different vs anthro or bedrock economically?
[04:30] Rahul Desai: short answer: we couple a high-throughput runtime with explicit levers (batching, prefix kv caching, quantization profiles) and give observable per-token cost breakdowns. other providers may offer models but not the same runtime optimizations or the same routing and rollback policies. bedrock ties to cloud provider pricing; we provide more predictable host/dedicated options and transparent unit economics for customers wanting to optimize cost at the application level.
[04:55] Maya Lin: we have about $15k/month target for proof-of-value in q3 — can we run a pilot that demonstrates hitting latency SLOs and shows cost per 1k requests with our prompts?
[05:05] Sofia Martinez: absolutely. typical pilot plan: 2-week bench + 2-week pilot in production shadow mode. rahul, what do we need from them to run bench?
[05:12] Rahul Desai: we need an anonymized prompt set (1k-5k sample), target latency SLO (p50/p99), qps profile (baseline and peak window), and region preference. we'll run tests across hosted and dedicated variants and return a side-by-side TCO.
[05:24] Jordan Reeves: for private on-prem, what's the ops burden — we can't be 24/7 on-call for kernel-level issues.
[05:30] Rahul Desai: private is heavier — you manage infra, but we offer an enterprise support package for managed on-call and patching. dedicated gives a middle ground: we manage runtime and infra in a reserved pool, you get control but offload ops.
[05:42] Maya Lin: any quick wins for cost before a dedicated commit? like prompt engineering or quantization?
[05:47] Rahul Desai: prompt engineering to reduce output length is immediate. quantization (e.g., 4-bit) yields big throughput improvements and lowers instance memory, letting you pack more workers per GPU — that's often a 20-40% unit cost reduction with small quality tradeoffs depending on model.
[05:59] Ethan Park: what's your billing granularity? per request? per token? per minute for dedicated?
[06:04] Sofia Martinez: hosted is per token (and per-embedding). dedicated is usually a monthly commitment for capacity (we attach an effective per-token calc for usage vs commit). we can show both models in the TCO spreadsheet.
[06:15] Maya Lin: latency SLO we're targeting is p99 < 350ms for the 95% of user-facing traffic and p50 < 80ms. achievable?
[06:22] Rahul Desai: depends on model and context length. with a quantized 7-13b and batching tuned for low-latency, that's reasonable. for larger models you'd need more powerful GPUs or a higher SLO. we'll run tests to validate.
[06:32] Jordan Reeves: networking — can we use VPC peering and private endpoints?
[06:36] Rahul Desai: yes for dedicated/private; hosted has private endpoints for enterprise customers and VPC peering in certain regions. we'll document region constraints.
[06:44] Ethan Park: procurement questions: what's minimum contract length for dedicated? any termination penalties?
[06:49] Sofia Martinez: standard is monthly or annual commits. annual has a discount; termination terms vary by tier — i'll put a stub in the contract starter and we can negotiate.
[06:58] Maya Lin: are there any real-world examples of customers that dropped unit costs dramatically with caching?
[07:03] Rahul Desai: yes — we had a fintech customer with heavy system prompts drop billable tokens by ~45% via prefix caching and a hybrid routing setup; their effective per-token spend halved when combined with a dedicated commit and quantization. i'll anonymize and share the case study.
[07:16] Sofia Martinez: ok i'm going to recap next steps quickly. we'll send a pricing deck and TCO sheet with hosted/dedicated/private columns, security pack (SOC2, KMS, SSO details), and an ask list for the benchmark: 1k prompt sample, qps profile, latency SLO, preferred region. rahul will propose benchmark windows. goldenrod will deciding on pilot timing and budget.
[07:34] Ethan Park: sounds good. timeline wise, we want a pilot to start early q3 — ideally first week of july — assuming procurement and security signoff.
[07:41] Sofia Martinez: noted. any final q's?
[07:44] Maya Lin: nothing immediate. thanks.
[07:46] Jordan Reeves: no, thanks everyone.
[07:48] Sofia Martinez: great, we'll follow up with the deck and security docs. thanks all.

End notes:
- References shared on call: pricing deck (link will be added), security pack (SOC2, audit log examples), benchmarking scripts (to be shared by rahul).
- Transcript includes occasional auto-transcription errors (product names, acronyms). follow-up materials will be authoritative.
